answer: The retained passages support that cryptocurrency can be property held on trust, but ownership and trust rights depend on the particular terms, consent and party relationship. The 2023 decision rejected a trust under the 2018 terms while preserving the non-consenting-customer exception. The 2025 decision recognised pooled beneficial interests for non-consenting customers, distinguished ETD holders’ breach-of-trust claims and rejected Samara’s claimed trust against Gatecoin. These conclusions do not establish that a Product Provider is a trustee or has fulfilled paragraph 10 of 26EC22. Transfer requires an applicable legal proposition, a justified comparison of relationships and actual product facts. Later treatment remains unresolved, and the scenario-seven inconsistency must remain open.

claims.inference: Text: capacity to be trust property is distinct from creation of a trust. The court’s conclusion concerning customers governed by the 2018 terms cannot be extended to all cryptocurrency holders.
missing_premises: The terms governing the particular customer and evidence of assent.
The complete reasoning needed to determine the precise scope of the holding.
claims.proposition: The 2023 judgment recognised cryptocurrency as property capable of trust but found no trust intention under the 2018 terms, preserving the non-consenting-customer exception.
claims.status: Supported by retained judgment passage; broader application unresolved

support.quote: Cryptocurrency is “property” and is capable of being held on trust
However, the terms of the 2018 T&C show that there was no certainty of intention to create a trust over the cryptocurrencies held by Gatecoin
Except the Non-Consenting Customers, the 2018 T&C applied to, and governed the relationship between all the Customers

claims.inference: Text attribution: the 2023 passage quotes principles summarised by Briggs J in Re Lehman Brothers. Deduction: labels and intermediary status alone do not establish beneficial ownership; the relevant bilateral relationship must be assessed objectively.
missing_premises: The actual agreements, commercial arrangements and property concerned.
A checked account of how the quoted principles were applied in the full reasons.
claims.proposition: Words such as trust, custody and ownership, and the existence of an agency or brokerage relationship, are relevant but not conclusive.
claims.status: Supported as quoted reasoning, not an independently verified general ratio

support.quote: The words used by the parties such as ‘trust’, ‘custody’, ‘belonging’, ‘ownership’, ‘title’, may be persuasive, but they are not conclusive in favour of the recognition of B’s proprietary interest in the property, if the terms of the agreement or relationship, viewed objectively, compel a different conclusion.

The identification of a relationship in which A is B’s agent or broker is not conclusive of a conclusion that A is, in relation to the property, B’s trustee, although it may be a pointer towards that conclusion.

claims.inference: Text: classification depends on platform access, instruction timing and contrary evidence. Deduction: a post-change ledger entry alone does not prove customer consent to the changed terms.
missing_premises: Customer-specific evidence of platform access, instructions and timing.

claims.proposition: The 2025 reasoning treats scenarios one to four as presumptively non-consenting and scenarios five and six as presumptively outside that category, subject to the specified evidence.

support.quote: The customers should be regarded as NCCs unless there is evidence to show that they have accessed or used the Platform to effect the transactions

The transactions described in the 5th to 6th scenarios on their face required the customers to access or use the Platform to effect them and, prima facie, the customers fall outside the definition of NCC.
However, if the customers are able to prove that they gave the instruction to Gatecoin before the Relevant Date or without using the Platform, they should be regarded as NCCs.

rival_readings: Scenario seven: paragraph 8 supports exclusion because the transactions did not exist; paragraph 95 facially permits NCC status on proof of earlier or off-platform instructions. Neither reading is silently preferred.
Transfer: Gatecoin supports investigating objectively established ownership relationships; a stronger reading that all Product Providers hold assets on trust is unsupported.

Paragraph 10 can be read principally as retaining ultimate responsibility, or in conjunction with surrounding requirements as requiring substantive performance. The supplied passages do not establish that allocation, an isolated supervisory act or a satisfactory outcome alone is sufficient.
